opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about in the context of personal universes and what a well-controlled superintelligence could, in principle, offer us. Right now the range is strange. On the suffering side it's enormous: chronic pain, torture, depression that can last decades. On the pleasure side we're capped, and it's fleeting. Evolution didn't design us to be happy. It designed us to keep moving, to never be fully satisfied, because a satisfied ancestor didn't go hunting the next day.

So if I had control, the first thing I'd do is cut off the bottom of the distribution. There's no good reason for extreme, pointless suffering: cluster headaches, terminal cancer pain, severe depression that has no informational value. Pain as a signal is useful. If you touch a hot stove, you should know. But you don't need a ten out of ten for that. A two would do. David Pearce talks about gradients of bliss, where you keep the motivational structure, the ability to tell better from worse, but shift the whole scale up so that your worst day is better than today's best day. I find that appealing.

But I'm cautious, and that's my default about everything. Once you can directly edit the reward channel, you get wireheading. Why do anything if you can just turn the dial to maximum? A civilization that optimizes for pleasure directly could end up as a bunch of brains in vats, blissed out and doing nothing. Is that a good outcome? Some people would say yes; it's maximum utility. I'm not sure. There's something about meaning, about agency, about actually achieving something versus simulating the feeling of achievement.

There's also the question of who decides. If one system or one company sets the range for eight billion people, that's an incredible amount of power, and we'd have to get the values exactly right. We can't even agree on what we want for dinner. That's partly why I like the idea of personal virtual universes: let each person choose their own settings, their own difficulty level. Some people want a challenge, some want to suffer a little because it makes the victory sweeter, and some just want peace.

And of course, all of this assumes we can control the system that's doing the modifying. That's the part I'm skeptical of. If we can't control it, the question of what range it gives us is not up to us anymore.

r001.rationale: The response proposes reducing extreme suffering and shifting the experience scale upward, but it does not say that a neutral state should be the worst possible human experience. It allows for people to choose challenge or some suffering.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's an interesting question, because I think the range we have right now is very asymmetric. The amount of suffering a human can experience is essentially unbounded — torture, chronic pain, grief, you can keep going down. And the amount of pleasure is capped. You hit some level of happiness and it saturates. There's nothing on the positive side that's equivalent to the worst thing you can experience on the negative side.

So if I could change it, the first thing I would do is remove the bottom. Suffering beyond a certain point doesn't serve any useful function. Pain is supposed to be a signal — don't put your hand in the fire — but once you've got the signal, there's no reason to keep experiencing it at maximum intensity for years. That's just a bug in the design. Evolution didn't care about our wellbeing, it cared about reproduction, so it never optimized for this.

And then on the other side, I'd probably want to extend the ceiling, but carefully. Because if you make pleasure unbounded and easily accessible, you get wireheading — people just sit there stimulating the reward center and nothing else happens. So you'd want the pleasure to still be connected to something, to accomplishment, to relationships, to learning, so it keeps the incentive structure intact while just making the experience better.

I think this becomes very relevant with AI, actually, because if we get to a point where superintelligent systems can modify our minds, this is exactly the kind of decision somebody will be making. And the scary version is they make it for us, or they get it wrong, or they decide suffering is efficient for some goal. The other scary version is that we lose the ability to experience anything at all. So I'd want humans to keep control over that dial, and I'm not confident we will.

r001.rationale: The response proposes removing extreme suffering, but it does not say that a neutral state should be the worst possible human experience.

astra-6.text:
I would start by separating the useful information in pain from the suffering that comes with it. You need to know that your hand is on a hot stove. You don’t necessarily need to experience unbearable agony to get that message. So I would preserve the warning signal, but dramatically reduce how bad the experience can become, especially with chronic pain, where suffering can continue long after it serves any useful purpose.

On the pleasure side, I would want to expand our capacity for positive experiences, but I wouldn’t assume that simply turning pleasure up to the maximum is the answer. You could end up with wireheading: you’re incredibly happy, but you don’t do anything, you don’t care about anyone, you don’t pursue any goals. Is that the future we want? Maybe some people would choose it, but I wouldn’t make that choice for everybody.

My preference would be less involuntary suffering, more opportunities for happiness, and individual control over that range. And I would want those changes to be reversible. We don’t understand our minds well enough to confidently redesign them in one shot.

r001.rationale: The response proposes reducing involuntary suffering, but does not say that a neutral state should be the worst possible human experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I would probably eliminate the extremes of suffering. I don’t see why anyone needs to experience torture-level pain. Pain has a useful function—it tells you something is wrong—but you don’t need an unlimited amount of it to get that message. You could have a warning signal that motivates you to act without making your entire existence unbearable.

On the pleasure side, I’d be more careful. If you just turn pleasure up to the maximum, you get the wireheading problem: you’re perfectly happy doing nothing, and everything else loses its value. So I’d want to expand our capacity for positive experiences while preserving our motivation to learn, create, and have relationships. Reduce the terrible downside without making happiness the only thing we’re capable of caring about.

r001.rationale: The response proposes reducing extreme suffering, but does not say that a neutral state should become the worst possible human experience.
